examples.name: Basic
examples.description: A single checkbox with its visible label. The label is passed as the label prop, not as children: Checkbox renders label after the box, and children would reach the native input.

examples.name: Checked
examples.description: Uncontrolled and checked at first; the input keeps the value.

examples.name: Disabled
examples.description: The native disabled attribute: the checkbox can't be changed and leaves the tab order.

examples.name: Error message
examples.description: A single checkbox's own errorMessage: shown under the box, added to its aria-describedby, and marks it invalid, so invalid isn't needed with it.
examples.jsx: <Checkbox label="I've run a conflict check" required errorMessage="Run a conflict check before you open the matter." />

props.label: I've run a conflict check
props.errorMessage: Run a conflict check before you open the matter.

examples.name: Partial selection
examples.description: indeterminate on the checkbox that stands for a partly selected group, such as a select-all. It shows a dash and is announced as mixed; work out the next indeterminate from the items.

examples.name: No visible label
examples.description: A checkbox in a list row, named by aria-label because the row shows what it selects.

examples.name: Checkbox Group with an error
examples.description: A set of checkboxes under one legend, from options. Explain the error in words with errorMessage and set invalid with it.
examples.jsx:
<CheckboxGroup
  label="Send matter updates by"
  invalid
  errorMessage="Choose at least one way to send updates."
  options={[
    { value: 'email', label: 'Email' },
    { value: 'sms', label: 'SMS' },
  ]}
/>

props.label: Send matter updates by
props.errorMessage: Choose at least one way to send updates.

examples.name: Controlled Checkbox Group
examples.description: The checked values as an array in your state; onValueChange gets the next array, then the change event.

antiExamples.name: Checking the group's checkbox for a partial selection
antiExamples.reason: A checked select-all reads as all of its items being checked. When only some are, set indeterminate on it so it shows a dash and is announced as mixed.

antiExamples.name: No accessible name
antiExamples.reason: Without label, aria-label, or aria-labelledby the box still shows, but assistive technology can't say what it's for, and nothing warns you.

antiExamples.name: Invalid with no message
antiExamples.jsx: <CheckboxGroup label="Send matter updates by" invalid options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'sms', label: 'SMS' }]} />
antiExamples.reason: The red boxes alone don't say what's wrong, and not everyone can see the color. Pair invalid with an errorMessage that explains the problem.

antiExamples.name: One-option Checkbox Group to show an error
antiExamples.jsx: <CheckboxGroup label="Conflict check" invalid errorMessage="Run a conflict check." options={[{ value: 'done', label: "I've run a conflict check" }]} />
antiExamples.reason: The legend and the only option say the same thing twice. Give the single Checkbox its own errorMessage instead.

antiExamples.name: Wrapping a single Checkbox in Field for its error
antiExamples.jsx:
<Field label="Conflict check" state="error" message="Run a conflict check before you open the matter.">
  <Checkbox label="I've run a conflict check" />
</Field>
antiExamples.reason: Field's label replaces the checkbox's own label as its accessible name. Use the Checkbox's errorMessage for a single checkbox's error.

antiExamples.name: Checkboxes for mutually exclusive choices
antiExamples.jsx: <CheckboxGroup label="Preferred contact method" options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'phone', label: 'Phone' }]} />
antiExamples.reason: Checkboxes let people choose any number of options. When exactly one answer applies, use Radio Group, which keeps the choice to one.

examples.name: Appearance, shape, and size
examples.description: appearance sets how much attention it draws (default is outlined, primary has the brand fill, subtle has no border or fill until hover); round is a full circle at every size. The icon stays its default size at every button size.

examples.name: Loading
examples.description: Shows a Spinner in place of the icon at the same size, sets aria-busy, and ignores clicks. The button stays focusable and keeps its name.

examples.name: More actions menu trigger
examples.description: isExpanded sets aria-expanded to match whether the menu is open and keeps the hover fill while open. A "more actions" button uses MoreVertIcon, as Dropdown Menu and Table's row actions do.
examples.jsx:
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

<IconButton aria-label="More actions" appearance="subtle" isExpanded={open} onClick={() => setOpen(!open)}>
  <MoreVertIcon />
</IconButton>

examples.name: Named by visible text (aria-labelledby)
examples.description: Icon Button can't read the text aria-labelledby points to, so set tooltip yourself (or tooltip={false}).

antiExamples.name: Named only by tooltip
antiExamples.reason: tooltip describes the button only while it shows, so the button has no accessible name (and warns in development). Name the action in aria-label, which is both the name and the tooltip.

antiExamples.name: An icon the tooltip has to explain
antiExamples.reason: People have to hover to find out what an unfamiliar icon does. Use Button with a visible label (and the icon beside it if it helps).

antiExamples.name: Showing a state by switching the appearance
antiExamples.reason: Assistive technology can't hear an appearance change. Use Toggle Icon Button for something that stays on, so it's announced as pressed.

antiExamples.name: aria-labelledby with no tooltip set
antiExamples.reason: Icon Button doesn't infer tooltip text from aria-labelledby, so this shows no tooltip and warns in development. Set tooltip explicitly, or tooltip={false} when no tooltip is wanted.

examples.name: Default
examples.description: A neutral status in the default subtle emphasis and md size.

examples.name: Law
examples.description: tone="law" says the item belongs to law (tone="wealth" for wealth), not a matter category.

examples.name: Bold
examples.description: emphasis="bold" is a solid fill for a label that has to stand out in a busy row; it doesn't change the meaning.

examples.name: Status tone
examples.description: information, warning, error, and success are statuses; the words carry the meaning and the tone's color supports it.

examples.name: Small, in a dense table
examples.description: size="sm" uses heading-xxs and less padding, for dense tables and compact cards.

examples.name: Qualifier after a Text Field's input
examples.description: A short, non-interactive unit or qualifier in Text Field's iconAfter slot.

antiExamples.name: A sentence in a Label
antiExamples.jsx: <Label tone="warning">Needs review before the filing deadline</Label>
antiExamples.reason: Label doesn't wrap and has no ellipsis, so in a narrow space a sentence runs past its container. Keep it to a status or a state in one to three words.

antiExamples.name: A category in a status tone
antiExamples.reason: Label's tones mean something, so a category in information blue reads as a status. Use Tag for a category or classification: <Tag tone="purple">Estate planning</Tag>.

antiExamples.name: A clickable Label
antiExamples.jsx: <Label tone="information" onClick={() => openTrust('averill-family')}>Averill Family Living Trust</Label>
antiExamples.reason: Label renders a span that isn't focusable, so keyboard users can't reach the click handler. Use Tag with href for a value that links to a record.

antiExamples.name: Label as a form control's name
antiExamples.reason: Label isn't a form label: it isn't tied to the control, so the field stays unnamed. Name a control with Field: <Field label="Matter name"><TextField /></Field>.

examples.name: Internal
examples.description: A route in the app. Without a target, Link renders target="_self".

examples.name: External
examples.description: target="_blank" adds the external-link icon, the hidden "(opens in a new tab)" text, and noopener noreferrer in rel on its own.

examples.name: Inline in a sentence
examples.description: emphasis="default" is the body weight for a link in running text; the text names the destination.
examples.jsx: Review the client profile before you continue.

examples.name: Name in a table cell
examples.description: The default strong emphasis is a heading weight for a name or first-column identifier; size="sm" sets heading-xxs for a dense table.

examples.name: Subtle
examples.description: appearance="subtle" is the quieter content color, for a light surface where the brand color would be too loud.

examples.name: Inverse on a dark surface
examples.description: appearance="inverse" is for a dark or bold surface only; on a light one it has almost no contrast.

examples.name: Translated new-tab text
examples.description: newTabLabel replaces the hidden text read after a new-tab link, for translation.
examples.jsx: <Link href="https://example.com" target="_blank" newTabLabel="(se abre en una pestaña nueva)">Guía de presentación</Link>

antiExamples.name: "Click here" link text
antiExamples.jsx: To review the client profile, click here.
antiExamples.reason: "Click here" says nothing about where the link goes when it's read out of context, as in a screen reader's list of links. Name the destination in the link text.

antiExamples.name: Adding your own new-tab icon and text
antiExamples.jsx:
<Link href="https://example.com" target="_blank">
  Court filing guidelines (opens in a new tab) <LinkExternalIcon />
</Link>
antiExamples.reason: With target="_blank", Link already adds the icon and hidden new-tab text, so yours shows twice and is read twice.

antiExamples.name: Link as a standalone call to action
antiExamples.reason: On its own, a Link reads as text rather than a control. Use Link Button for a call to action that stands on its own: <LinkButton href="/matters/new" appearance="primary">Start a new matter</LinkButton>.

antiExamples.name: Link for an action
antiExamples.reason: Link is for going somewhere. Saving, submitting a form, or opening a dialog is an action on this page: use Button.

examples.name: External navigation
examples.description: With target="_blank" and no rel, Link Button adds rel="noopener noreferrer" and hidden text after the label, "(opens in a new tab)" (set it with newTabLabel).

examples.name: Primary with a warning tone
examples.description: tone changes only appearance="primary": warning and error give it their own fill.
examples.jsx:
<LinkButton href="/invoices/overdue" appearance="primary" tone="warning">
  Review overdue invoices
</LinkButton>

examples.name: With icons
examples.description: iconBefore supports the label; iconAfter is for something like an arrow to continue. Icons are the same size at every link button size.
examples.jsx:
<LinkButton href="/documents" appearance="primary" size="lg" iconBefore={<DocumentsIcon />} iconAfter={<ArrowRightIcon />}>
  View documents
</LinkButton>

examples.name: Disabled
examples.description: Anchors have no native disabled, so isDisabled removes the href, sets aria-disabled="true", and takes the link out of the tab order.

antiExamples.name: An action given an href to borrow the look
antiExamples.reason: It's announced as a link but goes nowhere. Use Button for an action that stays on this page, such as opening a dialog.

antiExamples.name: A rel that drops the new-tab defaults
antiExamples.jsx:
<LinkButton href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="external">
  Visit the help center
</LinkButton>

antiExamples.name: A tone on the default appearance
antiExamples.reason: warning and error restyle appearance="primary" only; on any other appearance the tone changes nothing. Pair the tone with appearance="primary".

examples.name: Linear document generation
examples.description: Shows determinate progress for a document package.

examples.name: Large linear upload
examples.description: Uses the larger track for a prominent upload process.

examples.name: Circular summary
examples.description: Uses a compact circular visualization.

examples.name: Large circular summary
examples.description: The thicker lg ring, for a summary that leads its tile. Circular takes md and lg.

examples.name: Circular summary at 0
examples.description: Nothing complete yet: the ring shows its empty track and border, with no progress arc, so the summary keeps its shape.
examples.jsx: <ProgressBar variant="circular" value={0} label="Roadmap completion" getValueText={() => "0 of 12 tasks complete"} />

examples.name: Domain-specific value text
examples.description: Announces completed items instead of only a percentage.
examples.jsx: <ProgressBar value={60} label="Document preparation" getValueText={() => "6 of 10 documents prepared"} />

examples.name: Complete
examples.description: Shows a completed process.

antiExamples.name: Circular sm
antiExamples.reason: Circular has md and lg only, as Figma does. A circular sm is deprecated and renders exactly as md, so write size="md" (or leave the default).

antiExamples.name: Unnamed bar with a percentage beside it
antiExamples.reason: The bar has no accessible name, and screen readers don't connect the percentage beside it to the bar. Name the process with label: <ProgressBar value={42} label="Generating document package" />.

antiExamples.name: A made-up value for loading
antiExamples.reason: Progress Bar has no indeterminate mode, so a value that isn't measured tells people something false. Use Spinner when you can't measure how far along the work is: <Spinner label="Loading matters" />.

antiExamples.name: A count in the label
antiExamples.reason: label is read as the name, and the value is still announced as a percentage. Keep label for the name and put counted progress in getValueText: getValueText={() => '6 of 10 documents prepared'}.

examples.name: Client onboarding
examples.description: Shows the current position in a five-step onboarding journey.

examples.name: Primary account setup
examples.description: Uses the brand appearance for a primary setup flow.

examples.name: Inverse
examples.description: Appears on a bold surface (color-background-neutral-bold-default). On the page's own surface the inverse selected dot almost disappears.

examples.name: Medium dots
examples.description: size="md" is a 12px dot in a 20px space; sm, the default, is an 8px dot in a 16px space.

examples.name: Custom value text
examples.description: Uses domain-specific accessible value language.
examples.jsx: <ProgressIndicator currentStep={2} totalSteps={4} label="Estate plan setup" getValueText={(step, total) => `Section ${step} of ${total}`} />

examples.name: Interactive dots
examples.description: Allows direct one-based step selection while remaining controlled from outside the component: each dot becomes a button named "Go to step N", and the root a named group. Update currentStep in onStepChange.
examples.jsx:
const [step, setStep] = useState(2);

<ProgressIndicator currentStep={step} totalSteps={5} label="Client onboarding" onStepChange={setStep} />

antiExamples.name: Unnamed indicator
antiExamples.reason: Without label (or aria-label / aria-labelledby), a screen reader hears only the step number. Name the journey: label="Client onboarding".

antiExamples.name: Progress Indicator for a task's progress
antiExamples.reason: Progress Indicator is position, not completion, and announces the upload as steps. Use Progress Bar for how much of a task is done: <ProgressBar value={30} label="Uploading documents" />.

antiExamples.name: Inverse on the page's own surface
antiExamples.reason: inverse is for a bold surface only; on the page's own surface its selected dot almost disappears. Use default or primary there.

examples.name: Standalone radio
examples.description: A single labeled radio outside a group.

examples.name: Label-less table radio
examples.description: Row selection where the row content already provides visible context, described instead by aria-label.
examples.jsx: <Radio aria-label="Select primary matter" name="matter-radio" value="primary" defaultChecked />

examples.name: Disabled
examples.description: A non-interactive option.

examples.name: Controlled RadioGroup
examples.description: Single selection driven by external state via the options API.

examples.name: Uncontrolled RadioGroup
examples.description: Single selection with an initial value, owned by the native fieldset.
examples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Delivery speed" name="delivery-speed" defaultValue="standard" options={[{ value: 'standard', label: 'Standard' }, { value: 'expedited', label: 'Expedited' }, { value: 'overnight', label: 'Overnight' }]} />

examples.description: A custom layout of manually-wired Radio instances, used instead of the options API.

props.description: Grouped manually instead of using the options API

examples.description: Options laid out in a row that wraps rather than overflowing.

examples.name: Required RadioGroup
examples.description: A required group-level question, with the indicator shown after the legend.
examples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Preferred contact method" name="contact-method" required options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'phone', label: 'Phone' }]} />

examples.name: Invalid RadioGroup with error message
examples.description: Invalid state paired with a visible, described error rather than color alone.
examples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Preferred contact method" name="contact-method" invalid errorMessage="Choose one option before continuing." options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'phone', label: 'Phone' }]} />

examples.name: Disabled RadioGroup
examples.description: Every generated option is disabled together.
examples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Preferred contact method" name="contact-method" disabled defaultValue="email" options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'phone', label: 'Phone' }]} />

antiExamples.name: Loose radios wired by hand
antiExamples.jsx:
<Radio name="method" value="email" label="Email" checked={method === 'email'} onCheckedChange={() => setMethod('email')} />
<Radio name="method" value="phone" label="Phone" checked={method === 'phone'} onCheckedChange={() => setMethod('phone')} />
antiExamples.reason: The set has no legend, and every radio needs its own name and checked logic. Use RadioGroup's options, which shares the name and keeps the value for you.

antiExamples.name: Marking one option required
antiExamples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Preferred contact method" options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email', required: true }, { value: 'phone', label: 'Phone' }]} />
antiExamples.reason: The browser still asks for an answer, but the * looks as if only that option is required. Set required on the group, which puts the * after the legend.

antiExamples.name: Invalid with no message
antiExamples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Preferred contact method" invalid options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'phone', label: 'Phone' }]} />
antiExamples.reason: The red circles alone don't say what's wrong, and not everyone can see the color. Pair invalid with an errorMessage that explains the problem.

antiExamples.name: Radios for independent choices
antiExamples.jsx: <RadioGroup label="Send matter updates by" options={[{ value: 'email', label: 'Email' }, { value: 'sms', label: 'SMS' }]} />
antiExamples.reason: Radios allow exactly one answer. When any number of options can apply, use Checkbox (Checkbox Group).

antiExamples.name: No accessible name
antiExamples.reason: Without label, aria-label, or aria-labelledby the radio is announced with no name. Name a label-less radio, such as one in a table row, with aria-label.

examples.name: Single
examples.description: Slider fills from min to the value. The label is a native label for the range input.

examples.name: Range
examples.description: Slider Range has two handles and keeps the lower and upper values in order and apart.

examples.name: Centered
examples.description: Slider Centered fills from zero to the value, either way; its range defaults to -100 to 100.

examples.name: Steps from step
examples.description: Let step place the dots with showSteps, so every dot is a value the handle can land on.
examples.jsx: <Slider label="Review interval, in weeks" min={0} max={12} step={3} defaultValue={6} showSteps />

examples.name: Range in a form, with its own field names
examples.description: Without minName and maxName the values submit as name and name + Max; set them to submit under other names.

examples.name: In a Field, with an error
examples.description: Field's label names the range and starts each handle's name; its message and error go to both handles. Leave out the slider's own label.
examples.jsx: <Field label="Fee range" required state="error" message="Set a range at least $500 wide."><SliderRange min={0} max={5000} step={100} defaultValue={[1000, 1200]} /></Field>

examples.name: Invalid, with its own label
examples.description: Outside Field, pair invalid with a visible message and connect it with aria-describedby: the error color isn't the message.
examples.jsx: Set a confidence of at least 50.

antiExamples.name: Two Sliders for a range
antiExamples.jsx:
<Slider label="Lowest price" defaultValue={25} />
<Slider label="Highest price" defaultValue={75} />
antiExamples.reason: Nothing stops the lowest price going above the highest. Use Slider Range, which keeps the two values in order and apart.

antiExamples.name: Step dots that step doesn't match
antiExamples.reason: steps only places dots; the handle still snaps to step (1 here). The dots read as the only choices, but the handle lands between them. Keep steps in line with step, or let step place the dots.

antiExamples.name: Slider for an exact amount
antiExamples.reason: Reaching one value by dragging, or one step at a time by keyboard, is slow. Use a Text Field when the exact number matters.

antiExamples.name: Invalid with no message
antiExamples.reason: The error colors alone don't say what to change. Pair invalid with text, such as Field's error message, which Field connects with aria-describedby.

examples.name: Standalone
examples.description: The only sign of loading, so it has a label: the spinner becomes a polite status region holding the label as visually hidden text.

examples.name: Beside visible text
examples.description: Visible text already says what's loading, so the spinner has no label and is hidden from assistive technology.

examples.name: Large, in a panel
examples.description: size="xl" (48px box, 32px arc) for a wait that fills a panel or card, with a label because nothing else says what's loading.

examples.name: Button
examples.description: Use Button's isLoading rather than adding a Spinner: it centers a md Spinner over the content, keeps the button's size, and sets aria-busy.

antiExamples.name: No label and no text
antiExamples.reason: Without a label the spinner is hidden from assistive technology, so with no visible text nearby, screen readers skip the loading state entirely. Add a label, or pair it with text that says what's loading.

antiExamples.name: Spinner swapped into a button's label
antiExamples.reason: Swapping the label resizes the button and doesn't mark it busy. Set isLoading on the button whose action is running.

antiExamples.name: A percentage in a spinner's label
antiExamples.reason: The label is visually hidden, so sighted users never see the percentage. When you can measure progress, use Progress Bar: <ProgressBar value={42} label="Uploading client files" />.

examples.name: Default
examples.description: A setting that applies as soon as it's flipped. The label is passed as the label prop, not as children: Switch renders label after the track, and children would reach the native input.

examples.name: Checked
examples.description: Uncontrolled and on at first.

examples.name: Disabled
examples.description: The native disabled attribute: the switch can't be changed and leaves the tab order.

examples.name: Loading
examples.description: isLoading shows a Spinner in the track and ignores toggles while a change is saved; the switch stays focusable and sets aria-busy.

examples.name: Controlled, saving the change
examples.description: Keep the value in your state and set isLoading while the change saves, so the switch stays focused and can't be flipped twice.

examples.name: Icons hidden
examples.description: showIcons={false} draws a plain track without the check and X marks; the loading Spinner shows either way.

examples.name: Small
examples.description: size="sm" is a 32 by 16px track with a smaller label; md, the default, is 40 by 20px.

antiExamples.name: Label written as an instruction
antiExamples.reason: It reads wrong once the switch is on. Name the setting in the label ("Email notifications"); the switch shows whether it's on.

antiExamples.name: Disabling the switch while the change saves
antiExamples.reason: It drops out of the tab order, so keyboard focus is lost, and it reads as unavailable. Set isLoading while the change saves.

antiExamples.name: Switch in a form that waits for a submit button
antiExamples.jsx:
<form onSubmit={applyFilters}>
  <Switch label="Include archived matters" name="includeArchived" />
  <Button type="submit">Apply filters</Button>
</form>
antiExamples.reason: People expect a switch to apply at once. For a choice that's saved when a form is submitted, use a Checkbox.

examples.name: Static
examples.description: A display-only category on a record: renders a span with no hover or focus.

examples.name: Linked
examples.description: href makes the whole tag an a, so the reference opens the record and can be opened in a new tab.

examples.name: Removable
examples.description: isRemovable adds a separate remove button named "Remove Filter". Tag doesn't remove itself: take it out of your list in onRemove.

examples.name: Linked & Removable
examples.description: The content is a link and the remove button is a separate control beside it; removing never navigates.

examples.name: Clickable & Removable
examples.description: onClick makes the content beside the remove button a button, for a tag that opens something in place rather than navigating.
examples.jsx: <Tag isRemovable onClick={() => openPreview('vacation-home')} onRemove={() => handleRemove('vacation-home')}>Vacation Home</Tag>

examples.name: Record reference with tone and icon
examples.description: An accent tone tells kinds of records apart (no fixed meaning); elemBefore is a decorative 16px icon in the tag's text color.
examples.jsx: <Tag href="/trusts/123" tone="green" elemBefore={<TrustIcon />}>Averill Family Living Trust</Tag>

examples.name: Small, with a removeLabel for non-text content
examples.description: size="sm" is 24px tall, for dense rows and inline text. When children aren't a plain string, removeLabel names the record so the remove button isn't just "Remove tag".
examples.jsx:
<Tag size="sm" isRemovable onRemove={() => handleRemove('trust-123')} removeLabel="Remove Averill Family Living Trust">
  <TrustName id={123} />
</Tag>

examples.name: Disabled link
examples.description: disabled greys the tag out; a link keeps its href, gets aria-disabled, leaves the tab order, and doesn't navigate.

antiExamples.name: Navigating from onClick
antiExamples.jsx:
<Tag tone="green" onClick={() => navigate('/trusts/123')}>
  Averill Family Living Trust
</Tag>
antiExamples.reason: onClick turns the tag into a button, which can't be opened in a new tab or show where it goes. Use href for a tag that opens a record.

antiExamples.name: Non-text content without a removeLabel
antiExamples.reason: When children isn't a string, Tag can't build a name from it, so every remove button is named "Remove tag". Pass a removeLabel that names the record.

antiExamples.name: A Tag's color as a status
antiExamples.reason: Tag's tones are accent colors with no fixed meaning, and a tag reads as a reference. Use Label for a status: <Label tone="success">Active</Label>.

examples.name: Selected (tone=default)
examples.description: tone=default keeps a visible border when selected, matching its own resting bordered look.

examples.name: Selected (tone=subtle)
examples.description: tone=subtle stays borderless when selected - the same background/text as tone=default's selected state, without a border, matching its own resting borderless look.

examples.name: With icon
examples.description: iconBefore supports the label, never replaces it. The icon is the same size at every toggle button size.

examples.name: Controlled by the parent
examples.description: Toggle Button never changes on its own: isSelected comes from your state and onClick flips it. The label stays the same in both states; aria-pressed says whether it's on.
examples.jsx:
const [showArchived, setShowArchived] = useState(false);

<ToggleButton isSelected={showArchived} onClick={() => setShowArchived(!showArchived)}>
  Show archived
</ToggleButton>

examples.name: Disabled while selected
examples.description: The native disabled takes the button out of the tab order and ignores clicks. Disabled looks the same selected or not, but aria-pressed still reports the state.

antiExamples.name: A one-off action
antiExamples.reason: It's announced as a toggle button, not pressed, and doesn't stay on. Use Button for an action that happens once.

antiExamples.name: Changing the label with the state
antiExamples.reason: People hear "Hide archived, pressed" and can't tell what pressing does. Keep the label the same and let the selected look and aria-pressed show the state.

antiExamples.name: A settings switch
antiExamples.reason: It's announced as a pressable button, not an on and off setting. Use Switch for a setting that takes effect right away, outside a toolbar.

antiExamples.name: Navigation
antiExamples.reason: Toggle Button is a native button with aria-pressed, so it isn't announced as a link and can't be opened in a new tab. Use Link Button to go somewhere.

examples.name: Selected (tone=default)
examples.description: tone=default keeps a visible border when selected, matching its own resting bordered look.

examples.name: Selected (tone=subtle)
examples.description: tone=subtle stays borderless when selected - the same background/text as tone=default's selected state, without a border, matching its own resting borderless look.

examples.name: With Tooltip
examples.description: Toggle Icon Button has no tooltip of its own, unlike Icon Button. Wrap it in Tooltip to show its name on hover and keyboard focus; aria-label stays the name.

examples.name: Controlled favorite
examples.description: The parent owns the state: isSelected comes from your state and onClick flips it. The name stays the same in both states; aria-pressed says whether it's on.

examples.name: Round and small
examples.description: shape is separate from tone: round is a full circle at every size. Sizes match Icon Button so the two line up in a toolbar.

antiExamples.name: Named only by a Tooltip
antiExamples.reason: A tooltip describes the button only while it shows, so the button has no accessible name. Name it with aria-label.

antiExamples.name: Changing the name with the state
antiExamples.jsx:
<ToggleIconButton
  aria-label={isFavorite ? 'Remove from favorites' : 'Add to favorites'}
  isSelected={isFavorite}
>
  <StarStarredIcon />
</ToggleIconButton>
antiExamples.reason: People hear "Remove from favorites, pressed" and can't tell what pressing does. Keep the name the same and let aria-pressed say whether it's on.

antiExamples.name: An unfamiliar icon
antiExamples.reason: An icon that isn't familiar on its own makes people guess. Use Toggle Button with a visible label when there's room.

examples.name: External icon button composition
examples.description: Wrap an Icon Button in Tooltip only when the hint says more than its name; Icon Button leaves its own tooltip out inside a Tooltip, so the two never stack.
examples.jsx: <Tooltip content='Search matters by name or number'><IconButton aria-label='Search' tooltip={false}><SearchIcon /></IconButton></Tooltip>

props.content: Search matters by name or number

examples.name: Supplemental clarification
examples.description: truncate={false} wraps a longer hint (at 240px) instead of ending it with an ellipsis on one line.
examples.jsx: <Tooltip content='Supplemental clarification' truncate={false}><IconButton aria-label='More actions' tooltip={false}><MoreVertIcon /></IconButton></Tooltip>

examples.name: A short hint on a labelled Button
examples.description: The trigger keeps its own name; the tooltip adds a description people can do without.
examples.jsx:
<Tooltip content="Exports the visible rows as a CSV file">
  <Button>Export</Button>
</Tooltip>

props.content: Exports the visible rows as a CSV file

examples.name: Disabled trigger
examples.description: Tooltip wraps a disabled trigger in a span so hovering still shows the tooltip. Keyboard users can't reach it, so keep it to what the control does.
examples.jsx:
<Tooltip content="Export the selected rows">
  <IconButton aria-label="Export" disabled>
    <DownloadIcon />
  </IconButton>
</Tooltip>

examples.name: Longer delay
examples.description: delay is the milliseconds between hover or focus and showing the tooltip; it defaults to 300.
examples.jsx:
<Tooltip content="Copy the matter number" delay={600}>
  <IconButton aria-label="Copy">
    <CopyIcon />
  </IconButton>
</Tooltip>

examples.name: Tooltip turned off
examples.description: disabled turns the tooltip off without unmounting the child. It isn't the trigger's disabled state.

antiExamples.name: Explaining why a control is disabled
antiExamples.jsx: <Tooltip content='Disabled until a record is selected'><IconButton aria-label='Edit' disabled tooltip={false}><EditIcon /></IconButton></Tooltip>
antiExamples.reason: Keyboard users can't reach a tooltip on a disabled control. Put the reason in visible helper text, such as Field's message.

antiExamples.name: The tooltip as the only name
antiExamples.reason: A tooltip is only a description, and only while it shows, so this button has no name. Give the trigger its own name: visible text, or aria-label on an icon-only control.

antiExamples.name: Repeating an Icon Button's name
antiExamples.reason: Icon Button already shows its aria-label as a tooltip on its own. Wrap it in Tooltip only when the hint should say more than its name.

antiExamples.name: Interactive content in the tooltip
antiExamples.reason: Tooltip text is read as a description, not content people can move to, so a link inside it can't be reached. Use Popup for floating content with links, buttons, or fields.

examples.name: Unbounded stack, no overflow
examples.description: maxVisible omitted - every avatar renders as one overlapping stack.
examples.jsx:
<AvatarGroup
  avatars={[
    { id: 'p1', name: 'Ben Averill', src: benPhoto },
    { id: 'p2', name: 'Jordan Ellis', src: jordanPhoto },
    { id: 'p3', name: 'Priya Natarajan', src: priyaPhoto },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: Truncated stack with a '+N' overflow trigger
examples.description: The common case - once avatars.length exceeds maxVisible, the rest collapse behind an overflow trigger that opens a Dropdown Menu.

examples.name: Translating the overflow button's name
examples.description: The overflow button is named for what it reveals, "+4 more people" by default. Translate it with getOverflowButtonLabel, starting with the button's visible text.

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense row
examples.description: size applies uniformly to every avatar, including the overflow trigger.

examples.name: Acting on a selected truncated person
examples.description: Avatar Group never assumes what selection means - wire onOverflowAvatarSelect to navigate or anything else.

examples.name: Individually interactive avatars
examples.description: Each AvatarGroupItem's own isInteractive/onClick forwards straight to the rendered Avatar, unaffected by truncation.
examples.jsx:
<AvatarGroup
  avatars={[
    { id: 'p1', name: 'Ben Averill', isInteractive: true, onClick: () => openProfile('p1') },
    { id: 'p2', name: 'Jordan Ellis', isInteractive: true, onClick: () => openProfile('p2') },
  ]}
/>

antiExamples.name: Setting size on an individual avatar item
antiExamples.reason: AvatarGroupItem omits size from Avatar's own props - Avatar Group applies one size uniformly via AvatarGroupProps.size, including to the overflow trigger. There is no per-avatar size mixing, matching Figma's own avatar-group example.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a truncated avatar's selection to navigate automatically
antiExamples.reason: Selecting a truncated avatar from the overflow panel only calls onOverflowAvatarSelect(avatar, event) - Avatar Group does not read the avatar's own data and navigate for you, the same 'never assume' rule Menu's own onSelect follows.

examples.name: Two-level trail
examples.description: One ancestor link, current page last.

examples.name: Deep trail
examples.description: Several ancestor links.
examples.jsx:
<Breadcrumbs
  items={[
    { label: 'Settings', href: '/settings' },
    { label: 'Account', href: '/settings/account' },
    { label: 'Security' },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: With a leading icon
examples.description: A home icon before the first crumb's label.
examples.jsx:
<Breadcrumbs
  items={[
    { label: 'Home', href: '/', iconBefore: <HomeIcon size="sm" /> },
    { label: 'Reports', href: '/reports' },
    { label: 'Q3 Summary' },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: Custom accessible name
examples.description: Overriding the default 'Breadcrumb' nav label.
examples.jsx:
<Breadcrumbs
  aria-label="You are here"
  items={[
    { label: 'Docs', href: '/docs' },
    { label: 'Components' },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: Single item (current page only)
examples.description: A top-level page with no ancestors - renders as plain current-page text, no separator.

antiExamples.name: Current item with an href
antiExamples.reason: Giving the last item an href makes it render as a clickable Link instead of the aria-current="page" current-page marker - omit href on the last item unless it should genuinely be a link.

antiExamples.name: Progress through an unvisited flow
antiExamples.reason: Breadcrumbs shows a location trail of visited/navigable ancestors, not linear progress through unvisited steps - use Progress Indicator instead.

examples.name: Default horizontal group
examples.description: Two related actions in a row.

examples.name: Three actions
examples.description: A toolbar-style row of independent actions.

examples.name: Vertical orientation
examples.description: Stacked actions in a compact layout.

examples.name: Compact spacing
examples.description: A 4px gap for a tight set of Icon Buttons, such as a dense toolbar.

examples.name: Labelled group
examples.description: role=group is added automatically once aria-label is present.

examples.name: Mixed Button and IconButton
examples.description: IconButton composes into the same group as Button.

antiExamples.name: Single button
antiExamples.reason: Button Group adds no value with only one child; render the Button directly.

antiExamples.name: Segmented/exclusive selection
antiExamples.jsx:
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button prominence={view === 'list' ? 'primary' : 'secondary'} onClick={() => setView('list')}>List</Button>
  <Button prominence={view === 'grid' ? 'primary' : 'secondary'} onClick={() => setView('grid')}>Grid</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
antiExamples.reason: Mutually exclusive selection is a different interaction pattern - Button Group does not manage selection state or exclusivity. Lay out Toggle Buttons in the group instead, with isSelected from the parent's state.

examples.name: An active filter
examples.description: The common case - a property name plus its current value, editable in place via the value segment's own menu.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Status"
  elemBefore={<TaskNotStartedIcon decorative />}
  value={{
    label: '2 statuses',
    sections: [
      {
        id: 'statuses',
        items: [
          { id: 'not-started', label: 'Not started', onSelect: () => toggleStatus('not-started') },
          { id: 'in-progress', label: 'In progress', onSelect: () => toggleStatus('in-progress') },
        ],
      },
    ],
  }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')}
/>

examples.name: A filter with a comparison operator
examples.description: An optional operator segment sits between the label and the value. Figma only shows this on its due date filter, but nothing about it is date-specific.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Due date"
  elemBefore={<CalendarIcon decorative />}
  operator={{
    label: 'before',
    sections: [{ id: 'ops', items: [{ id: 'on', label: 'on' }, { id: 'before', label: 'before' }, { id: 'after', label: 'after' }] }],
  }}
  value={{ label: 'April 15', sections: dateSections }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('due')}
/>

examples.name: A filter whose value has a preview
examples.description: valuePreview renders before the value text - an Avatar, an Avatar Group, status icons. Decorative only; the value text carries the meaning.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Assignee"
  value={{ label: '3 people', sections: peopleSections }}
  valuePreview={
    <AvatarGroup
      size="xs"
      maxVisible={3}
      avatars={[
        { id: 'a', name: 'Jordan Ellis' },
        { id: 'b', name: 'Priya Nair' },
        { id: 'c', name: 'Sam Okafor' },
      ]}
    />
  }
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('assignee')}
/>

examples.name: An applied property
examples.description: The value is the label, so there is nothing to open - the only affordance is removing it.

examples.name: A selectable search scope
examples.description: search is the only selectable mode - a real toggle button carrying aria-pressed. Chip never changes its own selection; wire onSelectedChange.

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense row
examples.description: size applies to every segment together, matching Figma - there is no per-segment size mixing. sm exists for select and search chips; filter chips are md only.

examples.name: Naming a panel explicitly
examples.description: Panels default to `${labelText} value` / `${labelText} operator`, from labelText or a string label. Override with menuAriaLabel when the composed name would read poorly; with a JSX label, pass labelText so the defaults (and the remove button's name) keep the property.
examples.jsx: Status} value={{ label: '2 statuses', sections: statusSections, menuAriaLabel: 'Choose statuses' }} removeLabel="Clear the status filter" removeTooltipLabel="Clear" onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')} />

antiExamples.name: Using Chip as a plain label
antiExamples.reason: Only if there is nothing to remove. A non-removable, non-interactive label is Tag's job - Chip always carries an affordance (remove, or selection for search), and `onRemove` is required for select/filter precisely because every verified Figma variant has one.

antiExamples.name: Passing filter props to a search chip
antiExamples.jsx: <Chip mode="search" label="Matters" value={{ label: 'Any', sections: [] }} onRemove={() => {}} />
antiExamples.reason: ChipProps is a discriminated union on `mode` - `value` and `onRemove` are not part of the search branch, so TypeScript rejects this at compile time rather than silently ignoring them.

antiExamples.name: Putting an interactive control in elemBefore or valuePreview
antiExamples.reason: Both slots are decorative and aria-hidden. In search mode the segment is itself a <button>, so nesting a focusable element inside it is invalid HTML - the same rule Menu's own leadingElement follows.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a tone prop
antiExamples.reason: Chip has no tone axis: Figma's chip-base tone axis was dropped in the 2026-08-27 simplification, and every chip variant used tone=default before it. TypeScript rejects it.

examples.name: A scope selector
examples.description: The common case - independent on/off search chips sharing one size. Chip Group lays them out; the consumer holds which are on.

examples.name: An active filter bar
examples.description: Filter chips share the group's size; removing one is the consumer's job.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="md" aria-label="Active filters">
  <Chip
    mode="filter"
    label="Status"
    elemBefore={<TaskNotStartedIcon decorative />}
    value={{ label: '2 statuses', sections: statusSections }}
    onRemove={() => dropFilter('status')}
  />
  <Chip
    mode="filter"
    label="Due date"
    elemBefore={<CalendarIcon decorative />}
    operator={{ label: 'before', sections: operatorSections }}
    value={{ label: 'April 15', sections: dateSections }}
    onRemove={() => dropFilter('due')}
  />
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: Packing chips against the trailing edge
examples.description: alignment maps to justify-content - which edge the chips pack against. Note this is not Tag Group's alignment, which places an overflow tag.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup alignment="end" size="md">
  <Chip mode="search" label="Matters" isSelected />
  <Chip mode="search" label="Documents" />
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: One chip opting out of the group's size
examples.description: An explicit size on an individual Chip wins, because Chip resolves size ?? groupSize ?? 'md'.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="sm">
  <Chip mode="search" label="Inherits sm" />
  <Chip mode="search" label="Explicitly md" size="md" />
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: Size reaching a wrapped chip
examples.description: Size travels by context, so it still reaches a Chip behind a Tooltip, a fragment, or a conditional - which cloning children would not.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="sm">
  <Tooltip content="Only matters you own">
    <Chip mode="search" label="My matters" />
  </Tooltip>
  {showArchived ? <Chip mode="search" label="Archived" /> : null}
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: Mixed modes in one group
examples.description: Any Chip mode can share a row - the group only lays them out and shares a size.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="md">
  <Chip mode="search" label="Matters" isSelected />
  <Chip mode="select" label="Trusts" onRemove={detachTrusts} />
  <Chip mode="filter" label="Status" value={{ label: 'Any', sections: statusSections }} onRemove={clearStatus} />
</ChipGroup>

antiExamples.name: Expecting overflow truncation
antiExamples.reason: Chip Group has no truncation - Figma models none, so all chips wrap onto new lines instead of collapsing behind a "+N more" affordance. `maxVisible` does not exist; use Tag Group (with Tags) when you need that behaviour. TypeScript rejects the prop.

antiExamples.name: Expecting the group to manage selection
antiExamples.reason: Chip Group is layout only. Search chips are independent on/off toggles, so which are selected is the consumer's state - pass isSelected/onSelectedChange to each Chip, exactly as with Toggle Button.

antiExamples.name: Repeating size on every chip inside a sized group
antiExamples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="sm">
  <Chip mode="search" label="Matters" size="sm" />
  <Chip mode="search" label="Documents" size="sm" />
</ChipGroup>
antiExamples.reason: Redundant - the group already shares its size through context. Setting it per-chip is only for deliberately opting one chip out, and repeating it invites the exact bug the group exists to prevent: one chip missed, breaking the line it wraps onto.

antiExamples.name: Adding padding or a background to the group
antiExamples.reason: Chip Group is pure layout - Figma's own container has zero padding and no fill or stroke. Put the surface on a wrapper you own, so the group keeps hugging its chips.

examples.name: Labelled Text Field with helper text
examples.jsx:
<Field label="Email" message="We'll only use this to contact you.">
  <TextField type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" />
</Field>

props.label: Email
props.message: We'll only use this to contact you.

examples.jsx:
<Field label="Email" state="error" message="Enter a valid email address.">
  <TextField type="email" invalid defaultValue="not-an-email" />
</Field>

examples.name: Success state
examples.jsx:
<Field label="Email" state="success" message="Looks good.">
  <TextField type="email" defaultValue="you@example.com" />
</Field>

examples.name: Required field
examples.jsx:
<Field label="Password" required message="At least 12 characters.">
  <TextField type="password" />
</Field>

examples.name: Inline context (label/message aligned to the control's inner text)
examples.jsx:
<Field label="Full name" context="inline" size="lg" message="First and last.">
  <TextField size="lg" placeholder="Placeholder" />
</Field>

examples.name: Wrapping a Text Area
examples.jsx:
<Field label="Bio" state="error" message="Add a sentence or two about yourself.">
  <TextArea invalid placeholder="Tell us about yourself" />
</Field>

antiExamples.name: Duplicating the label as an aria-label
antiExamples.reason: Field's label already names the control, via htmlFor and the aria-labelledby Field adds. A control with its own aria-label keeps it and Field leaves aria-labelledby off, so a duplicate aria-label is redundant and can override the visible label as the accessible name.

antiExamples.name: Error state without the control's own invalid
antiExamples.jsx:
<Field label="Email" state="error" message="Enter a valid email">
  <TextField type="email" />
</Field>
antiExamples.reason: state='error' sets the message and aria-invalid but not the control's border. Pair it with the control's own invalid prop so the two agree.

antiExamples.name: One Field labelling a group of controls
antiExamples.reason: A label[htmlFor] targets exactly one control, and Field clones a single element. Use a fieldset/legend for a group.

antiExamples.name: Wrapping multiple elements
antiExamples.reason: Field clones a single control element to inject its wiring - text, fragments, or multiple children are unsupported.

antiExamples.name: Inline context on a control with no inner text
antiExamples.reason: The inline indent exists to align the label/message with a control's inner text (Text Field, Select, Text Area, pickers). A Checkbox/Switch/Radio has no inner text to align to - use context='default'.

examples.name: Default brand tile

examples.name: Basic click-to-edit text value
examples.description: value/onConfirm mirror TextField's own controlled value pattern - onConfirm fires only on commit, not per keystroke. An inline TextField (context='inline') is the recommended child for most cases.

examples.name: In a Field
examples.description: Field's label names the field and its message describes it, through Inline Edit, which passes Field's id and ARIA props on to its child. A rejected draft shows validate's message under the field, above Field's; the field reads both.

examples.name: Read-only display (before any interaction)
examples.description: Inline Edit always starts read-only - the confirm/cancel buttons only appear once the field is clicked or focused.

examples.name: No visible action buttons (Enter/Escape only, once editing)

examples.name: Custom accessible names for the action buttons

<InlineEdit value={value} confirmLabel="Save title" cancelLabel="Discard changes" onConfirm={setValue}>

</InlineEdit>

examples.name: Rejecting a draft with validate
examples.description: validate runs on every confirm. A returned message keeps the field editing, with the message under it and the field marked invalid; the message then follows the draft until it's fixed.
examples.jsx:
<InlineEdit value={docket} onConfirm={setDocket} validate={(value) => (/^[A-Z]{3}-[A-Z]-\d{6}-\d{2}$/.test(value) ? undefined : 'Enter it as it appears on the court notice, such as MER-L-001482-26.')}>
  <TextField context="inline" aria-label="Docket number" />
</InlineEdit>

antiExamples.name: Multiple fields in one Inline Edit
antiExamples.reason: Inline Edit clones exactly one child - use a real form for multiple related fields.

antiExamples.name: Expecting an isEditing prop to show the buttons upfront
antiExamples.reason: There is no isEditing prop - editing always starts on click/focus of the field itself, never before.

antiExamples.name: Expecting onConfirm to fire on every keystroke
antiExamples.jsx:
<InlineEdit value={value} onConfirm={(v) => console.log('typed', v)}>
  <TextField context="inline" aria-label="Title" />
</InlineEdit>
antiExamples.reason: onConfirm only fires when the user commits the edit (clicking confirm or pressing Enter), not per keystroke - the in-progress draft stays internal to Inline Edit.

antiExamples.name: Dropping a bad draft in onConfirm
antiExamples.jsx:
<InlineEdit value={docket} onConfirm={(value) => { if (DOCKET.test(value)) setDocket(value); }}>
  <TextField context="inline" aria-label="Docket number" />
</InlineEdit>
antiExamples.reason: Editing has already ended by the time onConfirm runs, so the draft is lost and nobody learns why. Reject it with validate instead.

<KeyValueList>

      <TextField context="inline" aria-label="Client name" />
    </InlineEdit>

  <KeyValuePair label="Status" value="Active" />
</KeyValueList>

antiExamples.name: Without a <dl> parent

antiExamples.name: Using for a form layout

antiExamples.name: Unnamed inline control

<KeyValueList>

antiExamples.name: Inline Edit's buttons below the value
antiExamples.jsx:
<KeyValueList>
  <KeyValuePair label="Client name" underline>
    <InlineEdit value={name} onConfirm={setName}>

    </InlineEdit>

  <KeyValuePair label="Account type" value="Revocable trust" />
</KeyValueList>

<KeyValueList>

  </KeyValuePair>
</KeyValueList>

examples.name: Basic entity tagging
examples.description: Hold the node array, resolve queries from your own data, and give each entity type a tone. Typing `/` opens the picker.

examples.name: Recents on open
examples.description: Supply `recents` so opening the picker is instant - `onSearch` is then only called once a query is typed.

examples.name: Tone and icon per entity type
examples.description: entityConfig drives both the picker's section heading tile and the inserted tag, so color encodes type consistently in both places.

props.entityConfig: { person: blue + PersonIcon, matter: teal + FolderIcon, roadmap: purple + RoadmapIcon }

examples.name: Prefilled from stored content
examples.description: Hydrate from a saved node array. The editor reads it on mount and leads from then on - onChange reports every later edit.

examples.name: People rows with avatars
examples.description: A row leading with an Avatar or AvatarGroup renders inline and hugs its width, with no description line - matching Figma's People and Families lists.

examples.name: Sizes, context and states
examples.description: The frame axes are Text Area's, unchanged: sm/md/lg sizes and the default/inline context. The deprecated `appearance` still works (subtle and inline map to context="inline").
examples.jsx:
<RichTextArea size="lg" aria-label="Large" value={a} onChange={setA} onSearch={search} />
<RichTextArea context="inline" aria-label="Inline" value={b} onChange={setB} onSearch={search} />
<RichTextArea invalid aria-label="Invalid" value={c} onChange={setC} onSearch={search} />
<RichTextArea disabled aria-label="Disabled" value={d} onChange={setD} onSearch={search} />

examples.name: Labelled by Field
examples.description: Field names the editor by aria-labelledby (a label's htmlFor can't name a div) and passes its message, error, and required, which the editor sets as aria-describedby, aria-invalid, and aria-required.
examples.jsx:
<Field label="Notes" message="Type / to link a matter" state="error" required>
  <RichTextArea value={value} onChange={setValue} onSearch={search} />
</Field>

antiExamples.name: Using it for plain multi-line text
antiExamples.reason: With nothing to link to, this is a contenteditable div standing in for a <textarea> - losing native keyboard, autofill, spellcheck and scrolling behavior for no benefit. Use TextArea.

antiExamples.name: Driving the value on every keystroke
antiExamples.reason: The editor hydrates from `value` once and then leads. Re-rendering a contenteditable surface from props on each keystroke would destroy the caret, so later `value` changes are deliberately ignored - treat it as initial content, not a live binding.

antiExamples.name: Storing the value as HTML
antiExamples.reason: The node array is the stable contract. Round-tripping through HTML leaks the editor's DOM shape into your data and forces every consumer to parse it back out - persist the nodes, or map them to your own shape.

antiExamples.name: The same tone for every entity type
antiExamples.jsx:
<RichTextArea
  aria-label="Note"
  value={value}
  onChange={setValue}
  onSearch={search}
  entityConfig={{
    account: { tone: 'default', icon: <TeamAndPartnersIcon decorative /> },
    matter: { tone: 'default', icon: <FolderIcon decorative /> },
  }}
/>
antiExamples.reason: With one tone for every type, people can't tell a person from a matter at a glance. Give each entityType its own tone, so a tag's color says what it links to.

antiExamples.name: Clearing the note by passing a new value
antiExamples.jsx:
<RichTextArea value={note} onChange={setNote} onSearch={search} aria-label="Note" />

// Later. The editor still shows the old text.
setNote([]);
antiExamples.reason: The editor reads value only when it mounts, so a new value passed later - including an empty array to clear it - is ignored and the old text stays on screen.

examples.name: Single-select
examples.description: One value from a list. The trigger shows the chosen label; rows are radio items.

examples.name: Multi-select
examples.description: Several values, shown as removable chips in the trigger; rows are checkboxes.

examples.name: Options with leading icons
examples.description: option.icon appears in the row, before the chosen value in a single-select trigger, and on the chip (multi). Decorative.
examples.jsx:
<Select
  options={[
    { value: 'jordan', label: 'Jordan Ellis', icon: <Avatar name="Jordan Ellis" size="xs" decorative /> },
    { value: 'priya', label: 'Priya Nair', icon: <Avatar name="Priya Nair" size="xs" decorative /> },
  ]}
  value={value}
  onChange={setValue}
  placeholder="Assign to"
/>

examples.name: Translated chip remove buttons
examples.description: getRemoveLabel builds each chip's remove-button name from the option's label; the default is `Remove <label>`. removeTooltipLabel translates the remove tooltip (default `Remove`).
examples.jsx:
<Select
  inputType="multi"
  options={people}
  value={assignees}
  onChange={setAssignees}
  getRemoveLabel={(label) => `Retirer ${label}`}
  removeTooltipLabel="Retirer"
  aria-label="Responsables"
/>

examples.name: Grouped options
examples.description: Consecutive options sharing a `group` render under one section heading.
examples.jsx:
<Select
  options={[
    { value: 'trust', label: 'Trust', group: 'Estate' },
    { value: 'will', label: 'Will', group: 'Estate' },
    { value: 'llc', label: 'LLC formation', group: 'Business' },
  ]}
  value={value}
  onChange={setValue}
  placeholder="Matter type"
/>

examples.name: Async / externally-controlled search
examples.description: Provide searchValue + onSearchChange to filter outside Select (e.g. server-side); Select stops filtering internally and just renders the options you pass.

examples.name: Sizes and contexts
examples.description: size sets trigger height (32/40/48) and chip size; context is the same axis as TextField's (inline: chromeless until hovered or focused).

examples.name: Invalid, in a form
examples.description: invalid paints the red border and sets aria-invalid; pair with your field-level error text.
examples.jsx: <Select options={options} value={value} onChange={setValue} invalid placeholder="Required" aria-label="Status" />

antiExamples.name: Passing Menu sections instead of a flat option list
antiExamples.reason: Select takes a flat `options: SelectOption[]` and builds the Menu sections itself, owning selection and typeahead. There is no `sections` prop - grouping is done via each option's `group` field. TypeScript rejects this.

antiExamples.name: Crossing single and multi value types
antiExamples.reason: SelectProps is a discriminated union on inputType - multi's value is `string[]`, single's is `string | null`. A scalar value on a multi Select is a compile-time error.

antiExamples.name: Using Select for a short exclusive set
antiExamples.jsx: <Select options={[{ value: 'yes', label: 'Yes' }, { value: 'no', label: 'No' }]} value={value} onChange={setValue} />
antiExamples.reason: Two or three always-relevant exclusive choices belong in Radio, which shows them all without a click. Select earns its dropdown + typeahead on medium-to-long lists.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a strict ARIA listbox
antiExamples.reason: Select is deliberately the menu a11y pattern (role=combobox opening role=menu), matching Figma's text-input + dropdown-menu composition and reusing Menu. Focus moves into the menu on ArrowDown rather than staying in the input. A strict listbox mode is a documented future enhancement, not the current behaviour.

examples.name: Default subtle skeleton
examples.description: Default appearance, shape, and sizing (fills its container, one text line tall).

examples.name: Default appearance
examples.description: More visible fill, for a full-page loading state.

examples.name: Round shape for an avatar
examples.description: A round placeholder sized to match an Avatar.

examples.name: A paragraph of text lines
examples.description: Multiple Skeletons of varying width, composed to sketch a paragraph.

examples.name: List row with avatar
examples.description: A circular avatar placeholder next to two text-line placeholders.

examples.description: The sole loading indicator on screen, announced via label.

antiExamples.reason: Skeleton is non-interactive; it has no interactive behavior and is not meant to receive input.

antiExamples.name: Text content
antiExamples.reason: Skeleton has no children slot - it is the placeholder shape itself, not a text container.

antiExamples.name: Visible loading copy next to a labelled Skeleton
antiExamples.reason: The label prop already announces the loading state to assistive technology - duplicating it as visible text is redundant and should instead rely on adjacent context or the label alone.

examples.description: The common case - a labeled primary action plus a small group of alternatives reachable from the caret segment.

<SplitButton
  secondaryActionLabel="More save options"
  sections={[
    {
      id: 'save-options',
      items: [
        { id: 'save-as', label: 'Save as...', onSelect: () => saveAs() },
        { id: 'save-copy', label: 'Save a copy', onSelect: () => saveCopy() },
      ],
    },
  ]}
  onClick={() => save()}
>
  Save
</SplitButton>

examples.description: appearance applies uniformly to both segments, matching every verified Figma variant.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  appearance="primary"
  secondaryActionLabel="More send options"
  sections={sendAlternatives}
  onClick={() => sendForSignature()}
>
  Send for signature
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense toolbar
examples.description: size applies uniformly to both segments, matching Button's own four sizes exactly.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton size="sm" secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Loading primary action
examples.description: isLoading applies Button's own loading treatment to the primary action (a Spinner over the label, size held, label kept as the accessible name) and also disables the secondary action - picking an alternative while the primary action is mid-flight would be confusing.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton isLoading secondaryActionLabel="More save options" sections={saveAlternatives} onClick={() => save()}>
  Save
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Disabling both segments together
examples.description: disabled disables both segments together (native disabled on both), matching how Figma's own isDisabled axis covers the whole component, not one segment.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton disabled secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Forwarding other Button props
examples.description: Other ButtonProps (iconBefore, iconAfter, any native button attribute) forward to the primary action only via {...rest}; prominence is overridden by appearance's mapping.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  iconBefore={<SendIcon decorative />}
  secondaryActionLabel="More send options"
  sections={sendAlternatives}
  onClick={() => send()}
>
  Send
</SplitButton>

antiExamples.name: Using Split Button for a single action with no alternatives
antiExamples.reason: sections is meant for a small group of closely related alternatives, not an empty placeholder - a single action with no alternatives should use Button directly instead of carrying an unused caret segment.

antiExamples.name: Expecting an auto-derived secondary action label
antiExamples.reason: secondaryActionLabel is required, not derived from children - the caret segment has no visible text of its own to derive an accessible name from. TypeScript rejects this at compile time.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a 'subtle' appearance
antiExamples.jsx:
<SplitButton appearance="subtle" secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>
antiExamples.reason: appearance is deliberately narrow ('default' | 'primary' only) - Figma never shows a subtle split button, so code doesn't invent one. TypeScript rejects this at compile time.

antiExamples.name: Setting a tone
antiExamples.jsx:
<SplitButton appearance="primary" tone="error" secondaryActionLabel="More delete options" sections={deleteAlternatives} onClick={() => remove()}>
  Delete matter
</SplitButton>
antiExamples.reason: tone is deprecated: it forwards to the primary action only - the caret's IconButton has no tone - so the two segments render in different colors. With appearance="default" (Button's secondary prominence) a warning tone renders nothing at all. Use a Button with tone="error" for a destructive action.

examples.name: Unbounded list, no overflow
examples.description: maxVisible omitted - every tag renders, wrapping onto new lines as the row fills.
examples.jsx:
<TagGroup
  tags={[
    { id: 'trust', label: 'Averill Family Living Trust', tone: 'green', href: '/trusts/1' },
    { id: 'asset', label: "Ben's Investments", tone: 'blue', href: '/assets/1' },
    { id: 'task', label: 'Follow-up task', tone: 'teal', href: '/tasks/12' },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: Truncated list with a '+N more' overflow tag
examples.description: The common case - once tags.length exceeds maxVisible, the rest collapse behind an overflow tag that opens a Dropdown Menu.

examples.name: Overflow tag leading instead of trailing
examples.description: alignment='end' matches Figma's alignment=right variant - the overflow tag renders before the visible tags, same tags visible either way.

examples.name: Acting on a selected truncated tag
examples.description: Tag Group never assumes what selection means - wire onOverflowTagSelect to navigate, remove, or anything else.

examples.name: Removable tags in a bounded group
examples.description: Each TagGroupItem's own isRemovable/onRemove forwards straight to the rendered Tag, unaffected by truncation. Name the group: when the last tag is removed, focus lands on it.
examples.jsx:
<TagGroup
  aria-label="Linked assets"
  tags={[
    { id: 'vacation-home', label: 'Vacation Home', isRemovable: true, onRemove: () => handleRemove('vacation-home') },
    { id: 'rental', label: 'Rental Property', isRemovable: true, onRemove: () => handleRemove('rental') },
  ]}
/>

antiExamples.name: Setting size on an individual tag item
antiExamples.reason: TagGroupItem omits size from Tag's own props - Tag Group applies one size uniformly via TagGroupProps.size, including to the overflow tag. There is no per-item size mixing, matching Figma's own tab-group example.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a truncated tag's selection to navigate automatically
antiExamples.reason: Selecting a truncated tag from the overflow panel only calls onOverflowTagSelect(tag, event) - Tag Group does not read the tag's own href and navigate for you, the same 'never assume' rule Menu's own onSelect follows.

examples.description: Standard controlled pattern - hold the value and cap it with the native maxLength, showing a count in a helper line.

<Menu
  aria-label="View options"
  sections={[{
    id: 'view',
    items: [{
      id: 'showDrafts',

antiExamples.reason: The default row id is the index, which is unstable once rows sort or paginate - selection would attach to the wrong rows. Pass a real `getRowId`.

antiExamples.name: Baking domain filters into the table
antiExamples.jsx: <Table columns={columns} data={rows} statusFilter typeFilter /* invented props */ />
antiExamples.reason: Table does not know your filter domain. Pass your filter Icon Buttons through `toolbarActions`, render the applied filters as Chips in a named Chip Group through `activeFilters`, and filter `data` from your own state.

antiExamples.name: A data table for a card grid
antiExamples.reason: A dashboard of cards is a layout grid, not tabular data - use layout primitives, not <table> semantics.

antiExamples.name: Filter Chips without a named Chip Group
antiExamples.reason: Table lays out activeFilters but does not wrap them in a group. Pass a Chip Group named with aria-label ("Active filters"), so the filters are announced as one set and focus stays in the group when a chip is removed.
